{{Short description|Mathematical theorem that Linear Fnctions have Positive Extensions in Real Vectorspace}}
{{About||more theorems that are sometimes called Riesz's theorem|Riesz theorem (disambiguation){{!}}Riesz theorem}}

The '''M. Riesz extension theorem''' is a [[theorem]] in [[mathematics]], proved by [[Marcel Riesz]]<ref>{{harvtxt|Riesz|1923}}</ref> during his study of the [[Moment problem|problem of moments]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Akhiezer|1965}}</ref>

==Formulation==
Let <math>E</math> be a [[real number|real]] [[vector space]], <math>F\subset E</math> be a [[vector subspace]], and <math>K\subset E</math> be a [[convex cone]].

A [[linear functional]]  <math>\phi: F\to\mathbb{R}</math> is called <math>K</math>-''positive'', if it takes only non-negative values on the cone <math>K</math>:

:<math>\phi(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{for} \quad x \in F \cap K.</math>

A linear functional <math>\psi: E\to\mathbb{R}</math> is called a <math>K</math>-positive ''extension'' of <math>\phi</math>, if it is identical to <math>\phi</math> in the domain of <math>\phi</math>, and also returns a value of at least 0 for all points in the cone <math>K</math>:

:<math>\psi|_F = \phi \quad \text{and} \quad \psi(x) \geq 0\quad \text{for} \quad x \in K.</math>

In general, a <math>K</math>-positive linear functional on <math>F</math> cannot be extended to a <math>K</math>-positive linear functional on <math>E</math>. Already in two dimensions one obtains a counterexample. Let <math>E=\mathbb{R}^2,\ K=\{(x,y): y>0\}\cup\{(x,0): x>0\},</math> and <math>F</math> be the <math>x</math>-axis. The positive functional <math>\phi(x,0)=x</math> can not be extended to a positive functional on <math>E</math>.

However, the extension exists under the additional assumption that <math>E\subset K+F,</math> namely for every <math>y\in E,</math> there exists an <math>x\in F</math> such that <math>y-x\in K.</math>

{{Math theorem
| name = {{visible anchor|M. Riesz extension theorem}} 
| math_statement = Let <math>E</math> be a real vector space, <math>F\subset E</math> a subspace, and <math>K\subset E</math> a convex cone verifying <math>E\subset K+F</math>. Then every <math>K</math>-positive linear functional <math>\phi\colon F\to\mathbb R</math> has a <math>K</math>-positive extension to all of <math>E</math>.
}}

==Proof==
The proof is similar to the proof of the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]] (see also below).

By [[transfinite induction]] or [[Zorn's lemma]] it is sufficient to consider the case dim&nbsp;<math>E/F = 1</math>.

Choose any <math>y \in E \setminus F</math>. Set

:<math>a = \sup \{\, \phi(x) \mid x \in F, \ y-x \in K \,\},\ b = \inf \{\, \phi(x) \mid x \in F, x-y \in K \,\}.</math>

We will prove below that <math>-\infty < a \le b</math>. For now, choose any <math>c</math> satisfying <math>a \le c \le b</math>, and set <math>\psi(y) = c</math>, <math>\psi|_F = \phi</math>, and then extend <math>\psi</math> to all of <math>E</math> by linearity. We need to show that <math>\psi</math> is <math>K</math>-positive. Suppose <math>z \in K</math>. Then either <math>z = 0</math>, or <math>z = p(x + y)</math> or <math>z = p(x - y)</math> for some <math>p > 0</math> and <math>x \in F</math>. If <math>z = 0</math>, then <math>\psi(z) > 0</math>. In the first remaining case <math>x + y = y -(-x) \in K</math>, and so

:<math>\psi(y) = c \geq a \geq \phi(-x) = \psi(-x)</math>

by definition. Thus

:<math>\psi(z) = p\psi(x+y) = p(\psi(x) + \psi(y)) \geq 0.</math>

In the second case, <math>x - y \in K</math>, and so similarly

:<math>\psi(y) = c \leq b \leq \phi(x) = \psi(x)</math>

by definition and so

:<math>\psi(z) = p\psi(x-y) = p(\psi(x)-\psi(y)) \geq 0.</math>

In all cases, <math>\psi(z) > 0</math>, and so <math>\psi</math> is <math>K</math>-positive.

We now prove that <math>-\infty < a \le b</math>. Notice by assumption there exists at least one <math>x \in F</math> for which <math>y - x \in K</math>, and so <math>-\infty < a</math>. However, it may be the case that there are no <math>x \in F</math> for which <math>x - y \in K</math>, in which case <math>b = \infty</math> and the inequality is trivial (in this case notice that the third case above cannot happen). Therefore, we may assume that <math>b < \infty</math> and there is at least one <math>x \in F</math> for which <math>x - y \in K</math>. To prove the inequality, it suffices to show that whenever <math>x \in F</math> and <math>y - x \in K</math>, and <math>x' \in F</math> and <math>x' - y \in K</math>, then <math>\phi(x) \le \phi(x')</math>. Indeed,

:<math>x' -x = (x' - y) + (y-x) \in K</math>

since <math>K</math> is a convex cone, and so

:<math>0 \leq \phi(x'-x) = \phi(x')-\phi(x)</math>

since <math>\phi</math> is <math>K</math>-positive.

==Corollary: Krein's extension theorem==

Let ''E'' be a [[real number|real]] [[linear space]], and let ''K''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;''E'' be a [[convex cone]]. Let ''x''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;''E''/(&minus;''K'') be such that '''R'''&nbsp;''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''K''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''E''. Then there exists a ''K''-positive linear functional ''&phi;'':&nbsp;''E''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;'''R''' such that ''&phi;''(''x'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.

==Connection to the Hahn&ndash;Banach theorem==
{{main|Hahn&ndash;Banach theorem}}

The Hahn–Banach theorem can be deduced from the M. Riesz extension theorem.

Let ''V'' be a linear space, and let ''N'' be a sublinear function on ''V''. Let ''&phi;'' be a functional on a subspace ''U''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;''V'' that is dominated by ''N'':

:<math> \phi(x) \leq N(x), \quad x \in U.</math>

The Hahn&ndash;Banach theorem asserts that ''&phi;'' can be extended to a linear functional on ''V'' that is dominated by ''N''.

To derive this from the M. Riesz extension theorem, define a convex cone ''K''&nbsp;&sub;&nbsp;'''R'''&times;''V'' by

:<math> K = \left\{ (a, x) \, \mid \, N(x) \leq a \right\}.</math>

Define a functional ''&phi;''<sub>1</sub> on '''R'''&times;''U'' by

:<math> \phi_1(a, x) = a - \phi(x).</math>

One can see that ''&phi;''<sub>1</sub> is ''K''-positive, and that ''K''&nbsp;+&nbsp;('''R'''&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;''U'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''R'''&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;''V''. Therefore ''&phi;''<sub>1</sub> can be extended to a ''K''-positive functional ''&psi;''<sub>1</sub> on '''R'''&times;''V''. Then

:<math> \psi(x) = - \psi_1(0, x) </math>

is the desired extension of ''&phi;''. Indeed, if ''&psi;''(''x'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;''N''(''x''), we have: (''N''(''x''),&nbsp;''x'')&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;''K'', whereas

:<math> \psi_1(N(x), x) = N(x) - \psi(x) < 0, </math>

leading to a contradiction.
